             Acknowledgments

These notes were begun more than 10 years ago to supplement a series
of lectures I gave in Tokyo during 12-16 August 1985. My original plan
for the notes encompassed most of the present manuscript, but the
version I actually managed to complete before the lectures took place
included only chapters 1 and 2 and the first six sections of chapter 3. A
year later I added chapter 4, but the notes lay dormant for several years
thereafter until the encouragement of several people convinced me to
complete and publish the manuscript. I would like to thank as many of
these people as I can remember, including Werner Ballmann, Keith
Burns, Peter Buser, Etienne Ghys, Ursula Hamenstadt, Jens Heber,
Ernst Heintze, Mark Pollicott, Viktor Schroeder, Ralf Spatzier, Wolf-
gang Ziller, and especially Bob Zimmer. I am also grateful to the
referees for a critical reading of the manuscript and Jens Heber for his
thoughtful comments on chapters 3 and 8.
              Introduction

The goal of these notes is to present some of the developments that
have taken place in the study of manifolds of nonpositive sectional
curvature in the last 30 years, with particular emphasis on the general-
izations of the Mostow rigidity theorem for symmetric spaces of non-
compact type and rank at least 2. These include the higher rank rigidity
theorems of Gromov, Ballmann, and Burns-Spatzier ([BGS], [Ba2], and
[BuS]). I give special emphasis to the geometry of symmetric spaces of
noncompact type and rank at least 2 since these are the simply con-
nected model spaces for the nonpositively curved manifolds that I
consider in these notes. Of the higher rank symmetric spaces I single
out SL(n, ff /SO (n, lJ) for purposes of illustration, and I make a con-
scious attempt to work out the details of geometric concepts in this
case.
   For a different approach to manifolds of nonpositive curvature see
the books [BGS] and [Ba3]. For a survey of results on nonpositively
curved manifolds see also [EHS].
   There are some notable omissions in these notes, which exist because
of limitations of the author with respect to time, space, and expertise.
There is no general discussion of CAT(O) spaces or spaces that have
nonpositive curvature in the sense of Alexandrov. Gromov initiated the
modern study of such spaces in the early 1980s, and it has grown rapidly
since then. There is no discussion of the ways in which complex
differential geometry or partial differential equations have contributed
to the study of manifolds of nonpositive curvature. In particular I have
not discussed the rigidity theorems for compact locally symmetric mani-
folds of rank 1, for which the sectional curvature is strictly negative.
There are a number of impressive results of this type due to Corlette,
Gromov, Hernandez, Mok, Schoen, Siu, Yau, Yeung, Zheng, and oth-
ers. For a good discussion of the activity in this direction and a good
bibliography of literature see the survey article [JY7]. For a partial list
of relevant articles see [Col,2], [GS], [Her], [JY1-JY9], [JZI-JZ3],
[Mkl-Md4], [MSY], [Samp], [Siul-Siu3], [SY], and [YZ].
   Most of the recent rank-1 rigidity theorems use the theory of
harmonic mappings f: X -> Y, where Y is a metric space of nonpositive
curvature in the sense of Alexandrov. The basic theory of harmonic
mappings is presently being extended to this setting; see, for example,
2       Geometry of Nonpositively Curved Manifolds

[Jos 1-Jos 3] and [KS]. The application of harmonic mappings to
geometric problems was initiated 30 years ago by Eells and Sampson
[ES] and S. I. Al'ber [A]1,A]2] in the case that Y is a Riemannian
manifold of nonpositive sectional curvature. In the most recent applica-
tions of harmonic maps the space Y is allowed to be something more
general, such as a Tits building, which occurs in [GS].
    Many of the rank-I rigidity results are in fact extensions of the
Margulis superrigidity theorem, which is not discussed in these notes.
See [Mar5] or [Z4] for a treatment of this result. The superrigidity
theorem can be applied to prove the arithmeticity of lattices and can
itself be proved by harmonic mapping techniques. One concludes that
lattices in semisimple Lie groups G with no compact factors are
arithmetic if G has R-rank k Z 2 (the original result of Margulis) or if
G is the isometry group of the quaternionic hyperbolic space or the
Cayley hyperbolic space (work of Corlette and Gromov-Schoen). It is
known that the groups SO(n,1) and SU(n,1), the groups of isometries
of the real and complex hyperbolic spaces, admit nonarithmetic lattices
and superrigidity also fails in these cases.
   Having discussed at some length what is not in these notes, I wish to
describe the organization and contents of this manuscript. There are 10
chapters, each of which is preceded by a detailed table of contents.
Chapters 2, 3, and 4 are followed by appendices that contain proofs of
results not given in the main text. At the end of the manuscript there is
an index of notation that lists the most important points in the text
where the notation is used. Following the index of notation is the index
of definitions and terminology with similar references to the places in
the text where each is used.
   I now describe the manuscript chapter by chapter. Chapter 1 con-
tains an introduction to the basic structure of manifolds of nonpositive
sectional curvature, especially the simply connected ones. All Rieman-
nian manifolds considered are assumed to be complete and connected
unless specified otherwise. Simply connected manifolds of nonpositive
sectional curvature are diffeomorphic to Euclidean spaces of the same
dimension, and they share many of the same convexity properties of
Euclidean spaces. Using convexity properties to prove geometric results
for simply connected manifolds of nonpositive sectional curvature was
first employed systematically by R. Bishop and B. O'Neill in [BO], but
the importance of convexity for symmetric spaces of noncompact type
was already known to Karpelevic ([Ka]) and Mostow ([Mos2]).
    Another useful tool for studying simply connected manifolds a of
nonpositive sectional curvature is the construction of a boundary sphere
M(oo) together with a natural topology such that the isometrics of A?
extend to homeomorphisms of R0). The topological nature of the
action of the isometry group 1(M) on M(-) reflects strongly the
                                                       Introduction       3

geometric properties of M and its quotient manifolds, particularly when
the group 1(M) satisfies the duality condition as defined in section (1.9).
The group 1(M) always satisfies the duality condition if M is the
universal cover of a complete manifold M of finite volume. The basic
properties of the boundary sphere Moo) were first developed in [EO]
and [E2], but these properties were known earlier to Karpelevic [Ka] in
the case that M is a symmetric space of noncompact type. The discus-
sion of the boundary sphere M(-) also uses earlier work and synthetic
methods of H. Busemann in a significant way.
   Chapter 2 contains a detailed study of the basic geometric structure
of symmetric spaces A? of noncompact type and rank at least 2. Such
spaces can be regarded as coset spaces G/K, where G =10(M ), the
identity component of the isometry group of M, and K is a maximal
compact subgroup of G. The group G is semisimple and has no
compact normal subgroups except the identity. I describe the geometry
of M by means of a Cartan decomposition fl = f + p of the Lie algebra
of G = 10(M) and especially by means of the root space decomposition
of g defined in section (2.7). 1 give the descriptions in terms of linear
algebra, and these descriptions become particularly concrete for our
canonical example, M = SL(n, I)/SO (n, R), discussed in (2.13).
   To illustrate, I give a very brief discussion of the geometry of a
symmetric space M of noncompact type. Each point p of M defines a

Here t is the Lie algebra of the maximal compact subgroup K = (g E
G : g(p) = p), and p is the orthogonal complement of f in fl with

and f are orthogonal with respect to B. The tangent space of M at p
can be identified with p, and if M is not a Riemannian product of
manifolds of lower dimension, then the inner product of M on its
tangent space at p is a positive multiple of the Killing form restricted to
p. The geodesics of M that start at p are the curves y. (1) = exp(tXX p),
where X is a nonzero vector of p and exp: R - G denotes the Lie
group exponential map. If X, Y, and Z are arbitrary vectors in p, then
the curvature tensor at p is givcn by R(X, Y )Z = - [[X, Y], Z).
   If a is a maximal abelian subspace of p and k = dim a, then the
formula for the curvature tensor shows that F = exp(aXp) is a com-

independent of a and the point p of M. This integer k is called the
rank of M or the R-rank of G. One may reformulate the discussion
above in geometric terms: if k is the rank of M, then every geodesic of

   In section (2.191 I discuss the multiplicative Jordan decomposition of
an element g of G =1o(M), which extends the standard multiplicative
Jordan decomposition of an element g of SL(n,R). Each element g of
G can be written uniquely as a product g = ehu, where e is elliptic, h is
hyperbolic, u is unipotent, and e, h, and u all commute. The action of
elliptic, hyperbolic, or unipotent elements of G on M or M(x) is
relatively easy to describe. The fact that e, h, and u all commute allows
one to reduce geometric questions about an element g of G to the
same questions about the components e, h, and u. See section (4.1)
below for an illustration of this technique.
   Chapter 3 is devoted to questions related to the geometry in M(x) of
the Tits pseudometric Td as defined by Gromov in [BGS]. The first five
sections of chapter 3 summarize basic properties of Td, and the reader
should consult [BGS] for further details. In section (3.6) I study the Tits
geometry and the Tits partial ordering for symmetric spaces of noncom-
pact type. Sections (3.7) through (3.11) contain further results about the
Tits geometry of M(x) that are either useful for or directly related to
the proof of the Mostow rigidity theorem, which I present in chapter 8.
Sections (3.10) and (3.11) contain rigidity results expressed in terms of
the Tits geometry of M(x). See also [BGS]. In section (3.12) I give a
brief discussion of the boundary KM(x) introduced by Karpelevic in
[Ka] for symmetric spaces of noncompact type and rank at least 2.

   In chapter 8, I discuss the Mostow rigidity theorem and give two
statements of this result whose equivalence I treat in some detail. The
proof I present is Mostow's, but I have rewritten parts of it to take
advantage of the geometry of M(-) discussed earlier. In particular I use
sections (3.7) through (3.11) in this treatment of the rigidity theorem.
    In chapter 9, I discuss a number of rigidity theorems and other
characterizations of symmetric spaces of noncompact type by various
geometric properties of a complete, simply connected manifold A? of
nonpositive sectional curvature. Many of these results were inspired by
or are generalizations of the Mostow rigidity theorem, and they include
the higher rank rigidity theorems of Gromov, Ballmann, and Burns-
Spatzier. The result of Ballmann and Burns-Spatzier may be stated as
                                                      Introduction      7

follows. Theorem: Let M be a complete manifold of finite volume whose
sectional curvature is nonpositive and bounded below. If the universal
Riemannian cover M is irreducible and has geometric rank k z 2, then M is
a symmetric space of noncompact type and rank k. The hypothesis that
the sectional curvature of M be bounded below was shown later to be
unnecessary in [EH]. Several of the results in this section are applica-
tions of the higher rank rigidity theorem stated above.
   In the concluding chapter 10, 1 discuss the relationship between the
algebraic properties of the fundamental group and the geometric prop-
erties of a compact manifold M of nonpositive sectional curvature. It
should not be surprising that such a relationship exists. If M is a
compact manifold of nonpositive sectional curvature, then Trk(M) = 0
for k z 2 since the universal Riemannian cover M is diffeomorphic to
Euclidean space. In particular, if two compact nonpositively curved
manifolds M and M* have isomorphic fundamental groups, then they
are homotopy equivalent. Results of T. Farrell and L. Jones [FJ1, FJ2]
show that homotopy equivalent manifolds of nonpositive sectional cur-
vature are homeomorphic but not necessarily diffeomorphic. It is a
basic principle that the topology and geometry of a Riemannian mani-
fold are closely related.
   In chapter 10, I present a number of examples of geometric proper-
ties that are determined by algebraic data in the fundamental group of
a compact manifold of nonpositive sectional curvature. These include
whether M splits as a Riemannian product (Gromoll-Wolf and Lawson-
Yau), whether M is flat (Bieberbach, Yau, Zimmer, and others), the
dimension of the Euclidean de Rham factor of M (Eberlein), whether
M admits immersed, totally geodesic flat tori of dimension k >_ 2 (Law-
son-Yau and Wolf), whether the universal cover 1l%f satisfies the Visibil-
ity axiom (Bangert-Schroeder), and whether M is irreducible and locally
symmetric of rank k >_ 2 (Ballmann-Eberlein). The last result follows
from the higher rank rigidity theorem of Ballmann and Burns-Spatzier
and the fact that the geometric rank of M equals the algebraic rank of
irl(M), which is an integer determined by algebraic data in irl(M).

1.1.    Notation
  We will use N to denote an arbitrary Riemannian manifold and N to
denote an arbitrary simply connected Riemannian manifold. We will
use M and M to denote respectively an arbitrary complete and an

the Riemannian metric d( , ). TN and SN will denote respectively the

to denote the unique geodesic of N with initial velocity v. We let (g`)
denote the geodesic flow in TN or SN given by g`(v) = y,'(t). In these

        Manifolds of nonpositive sectional curvature
  We recall the convention that M denotes an arbitrary complete
Riemannian manifold of nonpositive sectional curvature and M an
arbitrary complete simply connected manifold of nonpositive sectional
curvature. As we shall see the simply connected manifold M is diffeo-
morphic to a Euclidean space and there is a unique geodesic joining any
two points of such a manifold M.

1.3.   Examples

1.3.1. Geodesic symmetries and symmetric spaces
  For each point p of an arbitrary simply connected manifold M we
define a diffeomorphism Sp: M -i M by

DEFINITION. A simply connected manifold M is said to he a symmetric
space if for each point p E =-X1' the _geodesic symmetry SP: M - M is an
isometry of M. A symmetric space M is said to be of noncompact type if
M has no Euclidean de Rham factor.

Examples of nonpositively curved manifolds
1.3.2. SIMPLY CONNECTED EXAMPLES. (1) Euclidean spaces: The most
obvious examples are the Euclidean spaces with their canonical metric
of zero sectional curvature. These are clearly symmetric spaces.

   (3) Symmetric spaces of noncompact type: The hyperbolic spaces H"
are the simplest examples of symmetric spaces of noncompact type, but
there are many others. These spaces are the most important examples
of simply connected manifolds of nonpositive sectional curvature, and
an understanding of their geometry is very useful. We shall discuss
symmetric spaces of noncompact type in much greater detail in chapter
2. Here we outline an algebraic description of these spaces as coset
manifolds.
   If M is a symmetric space of noncompact type, then G =10(M) is a
semisimple Lie group with trivial center and no compact factors (see
chap. 2 for a proof). The group G acts transitively on M. If we fix a
point p in M and let K = (g e G: gp = p), then K is a maximal compact
subgroup of G and M is isometric to the cosec manifold G/K with a
suitable left-invariant metric. Conversely, if G is a semisimple Lie group
with finite center and no compact factors and if K is a maximal compact
subgroup of G, then the coset manifold G/K with any left-invariant
metric is a symmetric space of noncompact type. See also (1.13) below.
  The most important in some sense of the coset manifolds G/K
above is the example where G = SUn, O) and K = SO(n, R). If n = 2,
the space G/K is the hyperbolic plane. More generally, let M be a
symmetric space of noncompact type such that G =10(M) has dimen-
sion n z 2. Then after rescaling the metric of M by suitable positive
constants on de Rham factors, the manifold M can be isometrically
imbedded in SL(n, LJ)/SO(n, E) as a complete, totally geodesic sub-

manifold. See theorem (2.6.5) below for a precise statement of this
imbedding result whose proof may be found in the appendix of [E14,
prop. 19].
  (4) Homogeneous spaces: A Riemannian manifold N is homogeneous
if 1(N) (and hence !0(N)) acts transitively on N. In particular, any
symmetric space M of nonpositive sectional curvature is homogeneous,
but there are many simply connected nonsymmetric homogeneous
examples M.
   In [Hei2] it is shown that any simply connected homogeneous mani-
fold M of nonpositive sectional curvature admits a solvable group G* of
isometries that is simply transitive; that is, given two points q,, q2 E M
there is a unique element g of G* such that g(q,) = q2. In particular,
any homogeneous manifold M may be regarded as a solvable Lie group
with a left-invariant metric of nonpositive sectional curvature. Con-
versely, one may consider an arbitrary solvable Lie group G* together
with a left-invariant metric ( , ) and attempt to find necessary and
sufficient algebraic conditions on (G*, < , )} for the corresponding
sectional curvatures to be nonpositive. Following this approach Heintze
in [Hei2) took the first steps in a classification of all homogeneous
manifolds M of nonpositive sectional curvature. The classification was
completed by Azencott and Wilson in [AW1, AW2].

   (3) Quotients of symmetric spaces of noncompact type: It was known
for many years that Riemannian products of hyperbolic planes admit
compact and noncompact finite volume Riemannian quotient manifolds
that are irreducible in the sense of definition (1.2.1). See [Hi] and [Shim]
for a discussion of such spaces. The procedure for constructing such
examples is number theoretic. This procedure was generalized by A.

  (4) Quotients of homogeneous spaces: Perhaps surprisingly, the only
homogeneous manifolds M of nonpositive curvature that admit either
compact quotients or noncompact quotients of finite volume are the
symmetric spaces. This was proved first by Heintze in [Heil] for mani-
folds M with strictly negative sectional curvature and in the general
case by Azencott and Wilson [AW2, p. 28]. More generally, if _M is
homogeneous and I(M) satisfies the duality condition, then M is a
symmetric space by theorem 5.4 of [EC]. For a definition of the duality
condition see the discussion below beginning at (1.9.15).

1.5. Elementary properties of the fundamental group
     A simply connected manifold M is diffeomorphic to a Euclidean
space, and it follows from elementary facts about covering spaces that if
M is any complete manifold of nonpositive sectional curvature, then the
homotopy groups lrk(M) vanish for all k >_ 2. The homotopy of M is
therefore concentrated in the fundamental group, and M is a K(Tr,1)
manifold with Tr= ir,(M). It follows that the homology of M is the
same as the group homology of 7r,(M) (see [Br]). In particular, the
dimension, n, of M and the compactness of M can be read off from
 ir,(M): M is compact if and only if        ,(M),7L,) =12.
    Since the topology of M is contained in the fundamental group of M
in a certain sense, it becomes reasonable to ask what geometric infor-
mation about a complete manifold M of nonpositive sectional curvature
is contained in the algebraic structure of ir,(M). We shall consider this
question in much greater detail in chapter 10 for the case that M is
compact or is noncompact with finite Riemannian volume. In the
context of this problem a good general principle is that any result that
relates the geometry of M to the algebra of Tr,(M) should be examined
to see whether one can go backward, starting with an algebraic condi-
tion on or,(M) and concluding with a statement about the geometry of
M. See chapter 10 for examples.

tively curved manifold M is to regard Tr,(M) as a freely acting, properly
discontinuous group of isometries r of the universal cover M: M is then
just the quotient manifold M/t. One can then use information about
the action of 1(M) on M or on M(oo) (cf. (1.7.1)) to derive information
about Tr,(M). We give one illustration of this approach now.
 1.5.1. PROPOSITION. Let M be a complete manifold of nonpositive sec-
tional curvature. Then every element of the fundamental group of M has
infinite order, except for the identity.

1.6. Convexity properties of a simply connected space M
  Simply connected manifolds M inherit many of the important con-
vexity properties of Euclidean spaces. These properties are very power-
ful and are the basic tools that allow one to study manifolds of
nonpositive curvature. Most of these properties are shared by the more
general class of manifolds without focal points, which we will not
discuss. There exist manifolds without focal points that have sectional
curvatures of both signs (see [Gu]), but because of the convexity
properties that they share with manifolds of nonpositive sectional curva-
ture the expectation is that any result valid for nonpositively curved
manifolds will also be valid for manifolds without focal points.
   The convexity properties of M were first studied systematically by
R. Bishop and B. O'Neill in [BO, §§ 1-4]. For symmetric spaces an
independent treatment of many of these properties can be found in
[Most] and [Ka]. We sketch the most important of these properties and
refer the reader to [BO] for proofs.

Convex subsets of M and examples
   Since there is a unique geodesic of M joining any two given points of
M we define a subset of M to be convex (in the usual manner) if it
contains the unique connecting geodesic segment between any two of its
points. The closure in M of a convex set is also a convex set. A
Riemannian submanifold X of M is totally geodesic if every geodesic of
X is also a geodesic of M. A complete, totally geodesic submanifold X
of M is a convex subset of M. The next result is a partial converse and
shows that the general structure of a convex set in M is the same as a
convex set in Euclidean space. For a proof of this result see [CG, pp.
417-420].
1.6.1. THEOREM. Let A be a closed convex subset of a simply connected
manifold M of nonpositive sectional curvature. Then A is a totally geodesic
submanifold of M with possibly nonempty boundary. The set A is a
complete submanifold of M precisely when the boundary of A is empty.
   Next, we list some of the most important examples of closed convex
subsets in M. These are closely related to convex functions on M
(defined below in (1.6.4)).

1.6.2. ExAMPLES. (1) (Sublevel sets) If f : M - i8 is a continuous convex
function, then M. = (p E M: f(p) < a) is closed and convex for all
a c= R.
   (2) (Metric balls) For any point p in M and any number r > 0 the set
B,(p) = (q r= M: d(p, q) < r} is an open convex set. Its closure is a

closed convex set. This is also an example of (1) where f(q) = d2(p, q)

     (3) (Totally geodesic submanifolds) If A is any complete, totally
geodesic submanifold of M, then A is closed and convex. In particular,

The duality condition
   If the isometry group 1(M) of an arbitrary simply connected mani-
fold M is "large" in a suitable sense, then one can say a great deal
about the geometry of M and its quotient manifolds M. The definition
of "large" that seems most appropriate is the duality condition, which
we define in two different ways. It is interesting that even though
homogeneous manifolds M have a transitive group of isometries 1(M),
the group 1(M) is not large in this sense unless M is a symmetric space.
See theorem (1.9.18) below.

1.12.6. Examples of rank-1 manifolds
   Let M be an arbitrary manifold of nonpositive sectional curvature.
Then M has rank 1 in each of the following cases:
   (1) All sectional curvatures of 2-planes of M at one point p E M are
strictly negative (this implies that r(v) = I for all v E SP M by prop.
(1.12.1)).
     (2) M is a compact manifold of dimension 2 with negative Euler
characteristic (apply example (1) and the Gauss-Bonnet theorem).
  (3) The universal Riemannian cover M satisfies the Visibility axiom
and 1(M) satisfies the duality condition (this follows from theorem 2.6
of [BBE]).
   (4) M is compact and the geodesic flow in SM satisfies the Anosov
conditions (the Anosov conditions are equivalent to the condition that
r(v) = 1 for all v E SM by corollary 3.3 of [E5]).
   (5) Surgery examples of Heintze and Gromov (see the introduction
of [BBE] for details). These examples admit no Riemannian metric of
strictly negative sectional curvature.

1.12.12. Alternative definitions of rank
  The definition given above for the rank of a complete manifold M of
nonpositive curvature is not the only reasonable definition. One could
define the rank of a finite volume manifold M to be the largest rank of
an abelian subgroup of the fundamental group of M. This definition of
rank gives a value that is in general larger than the rank defined here.
For example, the rank-1 examples of Heintze have rank equal to
dim M - 1 in the sense just defined. The two definitions of rank agree if
the universal Riemannian covering M is a symmetric space of noncom-
pact type.
   Another possible definition of the rank of a simply connected mani-
fold M is the largest integer k =r*(M) such that M admits a k-flat.
The previous result says that r(M) s r*(M) if 1(M) satisfies the duality
condition. Equality holds if M is a symmetric space of noncompact type,
but in general, r*(M) may be larger than r(M) as the rank-1 examples
of Heintze and Gromov show. If M is a nonsimply connected manifold
of nonpositive curvature, then we define r*(M) to be r*(M), where M
is the universal Riemannian cover of M. If M is compact, then r*(M) is
at least as large as the largest rank of an abelian subgroup of the
fundamental group of M, and equality holds if M is real analytic, by
work of V. Bangert and V. Schroeder (see (10.3.18)). Work of M.
Anderson and V. Schroeder indicates that r*(M) depends only on the
algebraic structure of the fundamental group of M if M is compact

basic facts about the maximal compact subgroups of G.
1.13.14. PROPOSITION. Let M be a symmetric space of noncompact type,
and let G =10(M ). Then:

1.15. Convex subsets of spheres
      We state some results about convex subsets of the Euclidean n-sphere
with radius 1 for which the Riemannian metric is the angle function.
These results will be useful later in the discussion of Weyl chambers
and faces in chapters 2 and 3. These results are special cases of results
valid for complete Riemannian manifolds of sectional curvature K >- 0.
See chapter 8 of [CE] for further discussion of such manifolds.
1.15.1. DEFINITION. A subset X of the unit sphere S" c (f8"+' with its
canonical angle metric will be called convex if <(x,, x2) < IT for all points
x,, x2 E X and X contains the unique great circle in S" that joins x, to
x2.

1.15.2. DEFINITION. If X is a convex subset of the unit sphere S" with its
canonical metric we define the dimension of X(dim X) to be the largest
integer k with 05 k s n such that X contains a smoothly imbedded k-disk.
The interior of X(Int(X)) is the union of all smoothly imbedded k-disks
in X, where k = dim X. The boundary of X(dX) is defined to be
X - Int(X), where X denotes the closure of X in S". The boundary of
X may be empty.
REMARK. If X is a convex subset of the unit sphere S", then the
interior of X is also a convex subset of S" and is moreover a totally
geodesic, k-dimensional submanifold of S", where k = dim X. For de-
tails see lemmas 8.6 and 8.7 of [CE).
1.15.3. PROPOSITION. Let X be a closed convex set with nonempty bound-
ary of the unit sphere S" with its canonical metric.
   (1) There exists a unique point s(X) E Int(X) that is a maximum for
the function f: X - R given by f(x) = 4(x, OX) = inf(4(x, y): y e OX).
The point s(X) is called the soul of X.
   (2) If 46 is an isometry of S" (i.e., an element of 0(n)) that leaves X
invariant, then 0 fixes the point AX).
PROOF. Clearly, (2) is an immediate consequence of (1), and assertion
(1) is an immediate consequence of theorem 8.10 of [CE]. 0

In this chapter we sketch some relevant facts about symmetric spaces M
with nonpositive sectional curvature. We shall often omit details of the
proofs, referring instead to the appendix of this chapter, the appendix of

[E14], or one of the following general references for this section: [Hell,

219-232, 300-331], [Mil, pp. 109-117], and (Mos2, pp. 10-30].
2.1. DEFINITIONS. A simply connected manifold M of nonpositive sec-
tional curvature is said to be symmetric if each geodesic symmetry S.: M
- M is an isometry of M. If M is not the Riemannian product of a
Euclidean space [k, k >_ 1, with another manifold M*, then M is said to be
a symmetric space of noncompact type. It is well known that the property
of being symmetric (for a simply connected manifold) is equivalent to each
of the following properties: (a) VR = 0 (the curvature tensor is parallel) and
(b) if X(t), Y(t), and Z(t), are parallel vector fields along an arbitrary
geodesic y(t), then R(X(t),Y(t))Z(t) is a parallel vector field along y(t).
  We let G denote 1(,070, the connected component of 1(M) that
contains the identity, and we let g denote the Lie algebra of G.

g = (KILLING VECTOR FIELDS OF M). A vector field V of M is said to be
a Killing vector field if its flow transformations (0') are isometrics of M.
In our situation the flow transformations of a Killing vector field are
defined for all t r=- R. We may identify g, the collection of left-invariant
vector fields on G, with the collection of Killing vector fields on M as
follows: Given X E g we let VX denote the Killing vector field on M
whose flow transformations are {e`X}. This correspondence transforms
the Lie bracket in g into the Lie bracket of vector fields in M;
specifically - V X. Y  VX, VY ] for all X, Y E q. Hence we may regard g
as the Lie algebra of Killing vector fields of M.
   We shall investigate the algebraic structure of g below. We begin
with the following basic result.
2.1.1. PROPOSITION. Let M be a symmetric space. Then G acts transitively
on M. If M is of noncompact type, then G is a semisimple Lie group with
trivial center. Moreover, the Lie algebra g is a direct sum of simple ideals
9 1 ,. . .1 9 k such that [ g;, c 1 ] = 0 and B(g;, g,) = 0 for i # j, where B
denotes the Killing form of g. G itself is a direct product G, x G2 x  x
Gk, where G, is the connected normal Lie subgroup of G corresponding to
g;. None of the groups G; is compact (briefly, G has no compact factors).
PROOF. Let p and q be distinct points of M, and let y : [0, 1] - M be a
constant speed geodesic such that y(0) = p and y(l) = q. For each
t E [0, 1] let S, denote the geodesic symmetry S,(,) and let p, =        o So.
The curve t -p, is a 1-parameter group of isometrics of M such that
po = I and p,(p) = q. This shows that G(p) = M.

In particular, this shows that every geodesic y of M with y(O) = p has

   Next suppose that M is of noncompact type. We show that G has no
abelian normal subgroups A invariant under all continuous automor-
phisms of G. This will suffice to show that G is semisimple [Bou, part 1,
III, section 9.8, remark 1] and will also show that G has trivial center.
Suppose that such a subgroup A does exist. Then A would be invariant

group G satisfies the duality condition in M by the discussion of

nontrivial normal abelian subgroups.
     Since g is semisimple it can be written as a direct sum g =

i 0j. See, for example, [Hell, p. 122]. Since G has trivial center it is
routine to show that G is the direct product G, x x Gk, where G; is
the connected Lie subgroup of G corresponding to g;. The Killing form

the Killing form is negative definite on the Lie algebra of a compact
semisimple Lie group [Hell, p. 123].     0

2.12.   Weyl chambers in SM and M
   We construct two different types of Weyl chambers, each of which
determines the other. The first type, defined and studied in [BBE] and
[BBS], consists of regular unit vectors at a point p E M. Each point
p E M determines a set of Weyl chambers in SP M, the unit vectors at p,
and the union of all Weyl chambers at p is the set of regular vectors in
SPM. Any Weyl chamber in SPM is a fundamental domain for the
action of dG, G =1o(M), on the regular vectors of SM. The second type
of Weyl chamber consists of the union of all geodesic rays y,,(0, x),
where the unit vector v belongs to Weyl chamber of the first type at a
point p c- M. A Weyl chamber of the second type has p as a vertex and
is an unbounded, open convex subset of a k-flat in M, where k = rank M.

2.17.    Parabolic subgroups
   A subgroup G* of G =             is said to be parabolic if there exists
x E M(o) such that G* = G, = (g E G: gx =x). Unlike the subgroups of
G that fix a finite point in M, the parabolic subgroups are noncompact
and there is often more than one conjugacy class of parabolic subgroups
although there are still only finitely many. The parabolic subgroups G.,
                   Structure of Symmetric Spaces of Noncompact Type   101

determine the Tits geometry associated to the symmetric space M, and
we shall study this geometry both in this chapter and the next.
   For convenience we prefer to consider connected Lie groups, and for
this reason the statements of results usually refer to (G,),,, the con-
nected component of Gr that contains the identity, rather than GX
itself. The group G, is not connected in general as the next example
shows. We shall see below in (6) of (2.17.5) that G. has only finitely
many connected components for any point x E M(x). However, if
(GX) = (G,,) for points x, y e M(x), then G_, = Q. as we prove in (3) of
(2.17.25) below.

2.18. The geometry of M determines the algebra of g
   If we regard g as the Lie algebra of Killing vector fields on M, then
in principle we may recover the algebraic structure of g entirely from
geometric data in M. We shall illustrate this principle by constructing
geometrically the Cartan and root space decompositions determined by
a point p of M.
   Given a point p in M we let f = (X E g: X(p) = 0). If K = (g e
G: gp =p), then f is clearly the Lie algebra of K. Next we construct p
as we did in the beginning of this chapter. Namely, if y(t) is a constant
speed geodesic with y(0) = p, then we define the transvection p, =
S,,', o So, where S, denotes the geodesic symmetry at y(t). The elements
                    Structure of Symmetric Spaces of Noncompact Type           115

(p,) form a 1-parameter subgroup of isometrics of M, and they deter-
mine a Killing vector field P of g whose flow transformations are the
(p,). Let p denote the family of all Killing vector fields constructed in
this fashion. The family p is a vector subspace of g.

2.20.   Further remarks on totally geodesic submanifolds
        of M
   We continue the discussion begun in (2.6) and show that every
symmetric space M of noncompact type admits many totally geodesic
submanifolds through every point p of M. In particular, M admits
many rank-1 symmetric spaces, especially hyperbolic planes, as totally
geodesic submanifolds. Our main tool will be the root space decomposi-
tion of (2.7). Omitted proofs of results can be found in the appendix.

Joining points at infinity
   We conclude this section with some useful results whose proofs can
be found in the appendix. For a discussion in the special case that
M = SL(n, R)/SO(n, R) see (2.13.8) above.
   We recall from (1.11.1) that two points x, y e M(x) are said to be
joined by a geodesic y of M if y(x) = x and y(- x) = y or y(x) = y and
 y( - x) = x. If M is a symmetric space of rank 1, then the sectional
curvature of M is strictly negative, and any two distinct points x, y E
M(x) can be joined by a geodesic of M by proposition 4.4 of [EO].
Otherwise, we have the following.
                 Structure of Symmetric Spaces of Noncompact Type         151

2.21.13. PROPOSITION. Let M be a symmetric space of noncompact type
and rank k >- 2. Let x be any point of M(me), and let y be any point of Moo)
that can be joined to x by a geodesic of M. Let G = 10(M). Then:
   (1) The orbit G(y) is the set of points in M(c) that are G-dual to x in
       the sense of (1.9.12).
   (2) The set of points in M(c) to which x can be joined by a geodesic of
       M is the orbit Gx(y ), where G., = (g e G: gx = x).
   (3) The set G,,(y) is a dense open subset of the orbit G(y) relative to the
       topology on G(y) induced from M(oo).

result see Satz 3.1 of [I].

point p E M and a k -flat F such that F contains the maximal geodesics yp,,

Appendix                                                                        265




Given an arbitrary simply connected manifold M of nonpositive sec-
tional curvature, Gromov has shown in [BGS] how to construct a Tits
geometry on M(x) that generalizes the idea of the Tits building associ-
ated to a symmetric space of noncompact type. Our treatment in this
chapter up to (3.6) is almost entirely a sketch of section 4 of [BGS]. We
refer to that source for details and omit almost all proofs of the
assertions made.
  We define a metric Td on M(oo) that gives another measurement of
the flatness of the space M. This Tits metric Td agrees with the
standard angle metric of the unit sphere if M is a flat Euclidean space,
and Td is totally degenerate (i.e., Td(x, y) = +x if x # y in M(x)) if M
is a hyperbolic space or more generally a Visibility manifold. Here, by a
metric on M(oo) we mean a function d: M(x) x M(x)                          x) U {x)
satisfying the usual axioms but allowing the possibility that points may
have infinite distance.

Relationship between the geometry of M and the Tits partial
   ordering in M(x)
   In the remainder of (3.6) we show that several geometric properties
of M can be recovered from properties of the Tits partial ordering in
M(co). These properties include the degree of singularity of a point
x E M(), the rank of M, and the de Rham decomposition of M. Before
we consider these properties we show that the Tits metric and the Tits
topology (the .topology of the Tits metric) determine the Tits partial
ordering in M(x). Although this is logically redundant we include an
argument that the Tits metric determines the Tits partial ordering since
this argument is simpler than the corresponding argument for the Tits
topology.

Tits metric determines Tits partial ordering
  We show how one may recover the Tits partial ordering from the Tits
metric on M(x). See also appendix 5 of [BGS] for some discussion of
208      Geometry of Nonpositively Curved Manifolds

the relationship between the Tits metric and the Tits partial ordering in
the case that M has rank 2. I am grateful to Jens Heber who suggested
the approach used here.

Tits partial ordering determines de Rham decomposition
   Some geometric properties of a symmetric space M of noncompact
type and rank k z 2 can be obtained from information provided by the
Tits partial ordering.
3.6.56. PROPOSITION. The Tits partial ordering determines the rank of M
and the integers s(x), and e(x) for a point x E M(x).
PROOF. We recall from (2.21.7) that if x is a point in M(cc) and y is any
geodesic of M that belongs to x, then s(x) and e(x) are respectively the
dimensions of the noncompact type symmetric space factor and the
Euclidean factor of F(y), the totally geodesic submanifold of M that is
the union of all geodesics in M that are parallel to y.
   By lemma (3.6.18) and proposition (3.6.17), s(x) is the length of a
maximal chain that begins at x, where chain is defined in (3.6.16).
Hence s(x) is determined by the partial ordering. By (2.21.8) the integer
s(x) has k - 1 as its largest value, where k = rank M. Hence the rank of
M is determined by the partial ordering since it is one more than the
length of the longest chain in M(x). Finally, e(x) is determined by
the partial ordering since s(x) + e(x) = k for every x e M(x) by
(2.21.8).
   The main effort of this section will be spent proving that the Tits
partial ordering in M(x) determines the de Rham decomposition of M.
The precise result is stated below as proposition (3.6.65). To motivate
this result and to show the necessity of the conditions that occur in its
statement we begin with a discussion of geodesics in a product manifold
M and stability groups G, where G =10(M) and x e M(x).

3.8.   The Furstenberg boundary
   We now describe briefly a boundary of a symmetric space of noncom-
pact type, due to H. Furstenberg, that plays a key role in, among other
things, the proof of the Mostow and Gromov rigidity theorems discussed
later in chapters 8 and 9. There are several equivalent definitions of the
Furstenberg boundary. The most natural of these in our setting is the
definition found in [Mos2, pp. 31-341; see also [I].
   Let M be a symmetric space of noncompact type and rank k >_ 1. If
k = 1, then the boundary FM(x) that we define coincides with the usual
boundary M(x) so we assume that k >_ 2. Given a regular unit vector
v j=- Sp M we recall from definition (2.12.4) that a Weyl chamber W(y) c
M of the second type is given by

                  W(v) = {exp(ty*): v* E g'(v),t > 0),

where 1;'(v) c S,,M denotes the Weyl chamber of the first type deter-
mined by v as defined in (2.12.1). The point p E M is called the vertex
of the Weyl chamber W(v).
   We now define an equivalence relation of the Weyl chambers W(v),
v a regular vector of SM, which is the exact analogue of the asymptotic
236        Geometry of Nonpositively Curved Manifolds

equivalence relation on unit vectors of SM. See lemma 4.1 of [Most,
p. 331.
3.8.1. DEFINITION. For regular vectors v1, v, E SM we say that W(v1) is
equivalent or asymptotic to W(v2) if
                         Hd(W(vl),W(v,)) <x,
where Hd denotes Hausdorff distance (see (1.2.12)). We let W(vXx)

3.11.4. DEFINITION. Let M be a complete, simply connected manifold with

4.4.    Groups of isometries with fixed points in M(oo)
   Let M denote an arbitrary complete, simply connected manifold of

discussions see also chapter 7 and the appendix on the Tits metric of
M(x) in [BGS].
   We begin with a simple example. Let .0 E M be axial or parabolic,
and let r be the cyclic group generated by 0. Then any point in the
limit set L(1') is fixed by r. However, there are significant differences in

then by proposition (4.1.1) there exists a point x* E M,(x) such that
Td(x*, y):5 7r/2 for all y E M(x). This property, which we use as the
basis for the further discussion in this section, is not true for M ,(x) if 0
is axial.
4.4.1. DEFINITION. A group.!' c 1(i%1) is said to be admissible if Mr(x),
the set of fixed points in M(x) of r, is nonempty and if there exists
x* E M1.(x) such that Td(x*, y) :!f, it/2 for ally E Mr(cc)-
   If I' c 1(M) is abelian and contains only axial or elliptic isometrics

By theorem 1' of [GW] this discussion is also valid for solvable groups

   The situation is different if r c 1(M) is an abelian group that
contains nonidentity parabolic isometrics.
4.4.2. PROPOSITION. Let r c I(t f) be an abelian group that contains a
nonidentity parabolic element. Then 1' is an admissible group.

x(¢) E M4,(x) be the distinguished center of gravity of 46 as defined

 4.4.6. PROPOSITION. Let M be an arbitrary complete, simply connected

PROOF. Assertion (2) follows immediately from (1) by using corollary

H # (1). The set H is in fact a normal abelian subgroup of F by lemma

   The group H cannot have any fixed points in M; the set of points in
M that are fixed by H is a closed convex subset of M that is invariant
under t since H is normal in T. If H fixed a point of M, then it would
follow that M is the fixed point set of H since L(t) = M(co), contradict-
ing the assumption that H is not the identity. Therefore the dimension
of the flat submanifold F c M described above is positive, and the set

F/H is compact implies that L(H) = F(m) = B. Since H is a normal
subgroup of r it follows that r leaves B invariant. Therefore M is
isometric to the Riemannian product of F with another manifold by
proposition 2.2 of [Eli], which contradicts the hypothesis that M has no
Euclidean de Rham factor and completes the proof of (1). The proof of
the proposition is now complete.

4.4.7. PROPOSITION. Let M be a homogeneous space whose Euclidean de
Rham factor is trivial. Then either M is a symmetric space of noncompact
type or I(M) is an admissible subgroup and in particular I(M) fixes some

9.8, remark 11 there exists a nonidentity normal abelian subgroup A of
1(M). Note that L(I(M)) = M(oo) since I(M) acts transitively on M.
The fact that 1(M) is admissible now follows from proposition (4.4.6).

5.6.   Applications of the splitting criterion                        344




in this chapter we present a useful criterion for determining when a
simply connected Riemannian manifold of nonpositive sectional curva-
ture splits as the Riemannian product of two manifolds of lower
dimension. Our treatment is a modification of that found in [E15] and
[El 6], where a more complete discussion can be found. In this and later
sections we obtain applications of the splitting criterion.
   Let X = X, x X2 be a Riemannian product manifold, and let        and
9 be the foliations of X induced by the factors X, and X2. From the
discussion following (1.2.3) we recall the following.

5.1.    Isometries that preserve a Riemannian splitting

d 09(p) = l,((Ap) for i = 1, 2 and all points p E X.
   If ¢ E I(X) preserves the splitting X = X, x X2, then ¢ permutes

( p,(O), p2(0)) E 1(X,) x 1(X2) c I(X). If r cI(X) is a group of isome-
tries that preserves the splitting, then the projections p,: F - 1(X,) for
i = 1, 2 are homomorphisms.

5.2.   Symmetry diffeomorphisms
   Let A%1 be a complete, simply connected manifold of nonpositive
sectional curvature. For every point p E M there is a natural involutive
diffeomorphism SP: M -> M given by SP = exp c S o expp , where S:
TM - M is the map given by S(v) =_- v. Equivalently, SP(y(t)) = Y(- 1)
if y is any unit speed geodesic of M with y(O) =p (see (1.3.1)).
   The diffeomorphism SP: M - M is called the geodesic symmetry at p.
Clearly, (SP )2 = 1, SP fixes p, and dSP = -1 on Ti, M.

DEFINITION. We define groups G* and Ge* in Diff(M) by
  (a) G* is the group of diffeomorphisms of M generated by the geodesic
       symmetries {SP: p (=- M);
   (b) Ge* is the subgroup of G* generated by those elements {SP o S9:
       p,geM},
   Since the geodesic symmetries SP, p c- M, are all involutions it
follows that G* consists of all finite products SP, ° SP2 0 0 SP,,' where
the points p 1, ... , pN are chosen arbitrarily in M. Moreover, Ge* has
index 2 in G* and consists of all finite products S,, o SP2 o o S,,N,
where N is an even integer.
  The groups G* and Ge* are called the symmetry diffeomorphism
group and the even symmetry diffeomorphism group of M respectively.
   Note that M is a symmetric space if and only if G* c 1(M). If M is a
Euclidean space, then Ge4 is the translation subgroup of 1(M). If M is
symmetric of noncompact type (i.e., M has no Euclidean factor), then
one may show that Ge =10(M ).
   A geodesic symmetry SP extends naturally to a homeomorphism of
M(x) by defining SP(x) = y,x( - x) (cf. (1.7.10)). Hence we may regard
G* and Ge* as groups of homeomorphisms of M(x) with the cone
topology.


5.3.   Involutive subsets of M(c)
    A subset X of the boundary sphere M(x) is said to be involutive if X
is invariant under all geodesic symmetries SP, p C -M (see (1.7.10)).
    A priori we do not assume that an involutive subset is closed in the
cone topology, although this is often useful in applications. We list some
useful examples of involutive subsets.

EXAMPLE 1. Let M = MI X M2 be a nontrivial Riemannian product
manifold. Then the sets X, = M;(x) for i = 1, 2 are closed involutive
subsets of M(x).

In this chapter we consider isometry groups in a simply connected
manifold M whose Euclidean de Rham factor has positive dimension.
We are especially interested in the structure of lattices I' c 1(M) or
more generally subgroups IF c 1(M) that satisfy the duality condition.
The main results are theorems (7.2.1) and (7.3.3).

7.1.    Clifford translations

if the displacement function d., is constant on M. In this case 0 acts as
a translation on the Euclidean factor of M (cf. (1.9.4)).

8.1.1. THEOREM (Mostow). Let G and G* be connected, semisimple Lie
groups with trivial center that have no compact normal subgroups other
than the identity. Let r and r* be discrete, irreducible, cocompact

Let G have real rank k z 2. Then any isomorphism o: r -' r* extends to
an analytic isomorphism 0: G -+ G*.

the hypothesis that G have no PSL(2, f8) factor that is closed modulo r.
The hypothesis in the version above that r be irreducible implies by
(3.11.6) that G has no factor of any sort that is closed modulo r.
   Margulis has generalized the Mostow rigidity theorem to a super-
rigidity theorem. See chapter 7 of [Mars] and [Z1). In chapter 9 of these
notes we shall discuss rigidity theorems for compact manifolds of
nonpositive sectional curvature that are inspired by the Mostow rigidity
theorem. In particular, see the generalization by Gromov in theorem
(9.4.3).

The group r is irreducible if no finite index subgroup is a direct
product. Similarly, a compact locally symmetric space M is said to be
irreducible if no finite Riemannian cover of M splits as a Riemannian
product. If we write m = M/r, where M is symmetric of noncompact

admits a finite index subgroup that contains no elements of finite order
except the identity.

hypothesis of (8.1.1). A k-flat is r -periodic if F/rF is compact, where
rr = (y c- r: y(F) = F). If F is r-periodic, then by the Bieberbach

but no free abelian subgroup of rank r > k. Hence the isomorphism

In this chapter we discuss various generalizations of the Mostow rigidity
theorem that lead to differential geometric characterizations of sym-
metric spaces of noncompact type and rank at least 2. See also section 8
of [EHS] for a survey without proofs of such results. We avoid alto-
gether a discussion of rigidity theorems that generalize the rank-1 case
of the Mostow rigidity theorem. The methods in this case are com-
pletely different, and many beautiful results have been obtained, some
of which are described in section 8 of [EHS]. See also the discussion in
the introduction.
    We begin with two characterizations of higher rank symmetric spaces
that are proved in [E16]. We then continue with several characteriza-
400          Geometry of Nonpositively Curved Manifolds

tions of symmetric spaces of arbitrary rank from [Ell]. We conclude
the chapter with a discussion of the higher rank rigidity theorem of
Ballmann [Ba2] and Burns-Spatzier [BuS] together with a description of
several rigidity theorems that follow as consequences.

9.1.   Characterizations of symmetric spaces of higher rank
  The first result is theorem 4.1 of [E16].
9.1.1. THEOREM. Let M be irreducible, and let F c 1(M) be a subgroup
that satisfies the duality condition and leaves invariant a proper, closed
subset X of M(oo). Then M is a symmetric space of noncompact type and
rank at least 2.
PROOF. This is an immediate consequence of (5.4.4) and (5.4.5). The
topology of M(x) is the cone topology.
   Next we present a special case of theorem 4.3 of [E16].
9.1.2. THEOREM. Let M be a complete Riemannian manifold with sec-
tional curvature K :!g 0 and finite volume, and assume that the universal
cover M is irreducible. Then M is a symmetric space of noncompact type
and rank at least 2 if and only if the geodesic flow in the unit tangent
bundle SM fails to have a dense orbit in SM.
PROOF. Let r c I(M) be the lattice such that M = M/f. Since 1'
satisfies the duality condition it follows from theorem 4.14 of [E3] that
the geodesic flow in the unit tangent bundle SM has a dense orbit in
SM if and only if F has a dense orbit in M(oo). Hence if the geodesic
flow has no dense orbit in SM, then Al is symmetric of noncompact
type and rank at least 2 by (9.1.1). Conversely, if M is symmetric of
noncompact type and rank at least 2, then M(=) admits many proper,
closed subsets X that are invariant under 1(M) and in particular under
F. For example, let X be the set of singular points of M(oc) (cf.
(2.21.7)).

9.2.   Characterizations of symmetric spaces of arbitrary rank
   We present some results that can either be found in [Ell] or follow
from the work of [Ell]. The next result is contained in proposition 4.2
of [El 1], and the proof was later simplified in theorem E of [E151.
9.2.1. THEOREM. Let M have no Euclidean de Rham factor, and let
G c 1(M) be a closed, connected Lie subgroup of positive dimension
whose normalizer IF in I(M) satisfies the duality condition. Then there
exists a r-invariant Riemannian splitting M = MI X M, such that
   (1) M1 is a symmetric space of noncompact type and
   (2) G=10(M,)x{Id}.
              Characterizations of Symmetric Spaces of Higher Rank    401

   We shall sketch a proof of this result below. First we derive a
corollary, which is proposition 4.1 of [Ell].
9.2.2. COROLLARY. Let M be any complete, simply connected Riemannian
manifold with sectional curvature K:5 0 whose isometry group I(M) satis-
fies the duality condition. Then there exist manifolds M0, M,, and M2, any
two of which may have dimension zero, such that:
    (1) M is a Riemannian product M0 X M, X M2.
    (2) Mo is a Euclidean space.
    (3) M, is a symmetric space of noncompact type.
    (4) 1(M,) is discrete and satisfies the duality condition.

PROOF OF COROLLARY (9.2.2). Write M as a Riemannian product M0 X
M*, where Mo is the Euclidean de Rham factor of M and M* is the
Riemannian product of all other de Rham factors of M. Then I(M*)
satisfies the duality condition by (1.9.22) since 1(M) =1(Mo) x I(M*).
The desired result now follows by applying (9.2.1) to the group G =
10(M*) and using (1.9.22) to conclude (4).

PROOF OF THEOREM (9.2.1). Full details may be found in the proof of
theorem E of [E15], but for the convenience of the reader we give an
outline of the proof that conveys the main ideas. The proof rests on the
following facts:
    (i) G is a semisimple Lie group with trivial center and no compact
        normal subgroups except the identity.
   (ii) If L(G) = M(c), then M is a symmetric space of noncompact
        type and G =10(M ).
   (iii) Let r denote the normalizer of G in 1(M), and let
         (4 E 1r: og =g(k for all g r= G}. Then F0 = G Zr(G) has finite
        index in F.
  We sketch the proof of these facts. To begin the proof of (i) one
observes that if G is not semisimple, then it contains a nontrivial
abelian subgroup A that is invariant under all continuous automor-
phisms of G. Since r normalizes G it also normalizes A, and by (7.1.4),
A must consist of Clifford translations. This contradicts the hypothesis
that M has no Euclidean de Rham factor by (1.9.4). If Z denotes the
center of G, then Z is normalized by r, and (7.1.4) implies again that Z
consists of Clifford translations. Hence Z = (Id). The semisimple Lie

  It has been known for a long time that certain reducible symmetric
spaces M admit irreducible quotient manifolds of finite volume. For
example, if M is the Riemannian product of k >: 2 hyperbolic planes
with K = - 1, then there are classical procedures for constructing
irreducible, finite volume quotient manifolds, both compact and non-
compact. A sketch of one such procedure may be found in [Shim, p. 64].
   In general, a symmetric space M of noncompact type always admits
quotient manifolds of finite volume, both compact and noncompact, by
a result of A. Borel [Bo2]; see also [R]. However, if M is reducible, then
M does not admit irreducible quotient manifolds of finite volume unless
the de Rham factors of M are compatible in an appropriate way. This
compatibility of the factors is made precise in the next result due to F.
Johnson [J], which may be regarded as a complement to the previous
result. For the definition of irreducible see (1.2.1) and (3.11.4).

9.3. Higher rank rigidity theorem
   We refer the reader to (1.12) for the definition of the rank of a
nonpositively curved manifold. In this section we give a more complete
discussion of the result stated in (1.12.7).
9.3.1. THEOREM. Let hi be irreducible and have rank k >_ 2. If 1(M)
satisfies the duality condition, then M is a symmetric space of rank k.
9.3.2. COROLLARY. Let M be a complete manifold with sectional curva-
ture K 5 0, rank k >_ 2, and finite volume. If M is irreducible, then M is a
symmetric space of noncompact type and rank k.
   The first result in this direction was (9.3.2), which was proved by W.
Ballmann [Ba2] and K. Burns and R. Spatzier [BuS] under the addi-
tional hypothesis that M have a lower bound for the sectional curva-
tures. This hypothesis is automatically satisfied of course if M is
compact. The term "higher rank rigidity theorem" usually refers to
(9.3.2). The more general version (9.3.1) is proved in [EH].
  If M has finite volume, then m = M/r, where r c 1(M) is a lattice.
Hence 1(M) satisfies the duality condition since r does, and (9.3.2)
follows immediately from (9.3.1).
  Theorem (9.3.1) has been generalized to homogeneous spaces by J.
Heber [Heb].

9.4.3. THEOREM (Gromov). Let M) and M2 be compact Riemannian
manifolds with sectional curvature K:5 0 whose fundamental groups are
isomorphic. Assume that M, has no finite cover that splits as a nontrivial
Riemannian product and that the universal cover Ml is a symmetric space
with rank k >_ 2 and no Euclidean de Rham factor. Then M, and M2 are
isometric after multiplying the metric of Ml by suitable positive constants on
local de Rham factors.
410        Geometry of Nonpositively Curved Manifolds

REMARK. Gromov proved this result in theorem 14.2 of [BGS]. In the
special case that the universal cover M, is a nontrivial Riemannian
product, this result was also proved in [E131.
PROOF. By the Mostow rigidity theorem (theorems 18.1 and 24.1 of
[Mos2]) it suffices to prove that M2 is locally symmetric. We use the fact
that many geometric properties of a compact nonpositively curved
manifold are determined by the algebraic structure of the fundamental
group. This philosophy is the subject of chapter 10.
   We observe first that the universal cover M2 of M2 has no Euclidean
de Rham factor. This follows from (10.3.10), which states that the rank
of the Clifford subgroup of 7r,(M2 ), the unique maximal abelian normal
subgroup of ir,(M2), equals the dimension of the Euclidean de Rham
factor of M2. By hypothesis, M, has no Euclidean de Rham factor, and
hence the same is true for M2.
   Next we observe that M, and M, have the same rank k;-> 2. This
follows from (10.3.11), which states that the rank of M, equals the
algebraic rank of ir1(M,) for i = 1,2.
   The fundamental groups ir,(M,) and 7r1(M2) have trivial center by
(7.1.2) and (1.9.4) since M1 and M, have no Euclidean de Rham factor.
This implies that 7r,(M,) has no nontrivial direct product subgroup of
finite index. If it did, then M would admit a finite cover M* that splits
as a nontrivial Riemannian product by (10.3.9) below, which contradicts
the hypothesis on M,. Hence Tr 1(M2) has no nontrivial direct product
subgroup of finite index, and it follows that M2 admits no finite
Riemannian cover that splits as a nontrivial Riemannian product.
   If M2 is a nontrivial Riemannian product, then M, is locally symmet-
ric by the remarks above and (9.2.5). If M2 is irreducible, then M2 has
rank k > 2 by the discussion above and M2 is a symmetric space by
(9.3.2). The proof of (9.4.3) is complete.
     As an immediate application of (9.4.3) we obtain the following.
9.4.4. THEOREM. Let (M, g) be a compact, locally symmetric Riemannian
manifold with sectional curvature K< 0 and rank k >_ 2 whose universal
cover M has no Euclidean de Rham factor. Assume that M admits no finite
cover that splits as a nontrivial Riemannian product, and let g* be any
Riemannian metric on M with sectional curvature K :::-t, 0. Then (M, g*) is
isometric to (M, g'), where g' is a Riemannian metric on M that is
obtained by multiplying g by suitable positive constants on local de Rham
factors of M.
REMARK. If g' is any metric obtained by rescaling the metric g on local
de Rham factors, then clearly (M, g') has nonpositive sectional curva-
ture since (M, g) does. Theorem (9.4.4) says that this is the only way, up
to isometric equivalence, to obtain nonpositively curved metrics g' on
M.

One of the principles of Riemannian geometry is that the geometric and
topological properties of a Riemannian manifold X are often strongly
related, especially when X is compact. For a compact manifold of
nonpositive sectional curvature the homotopy information is carried in
the fundamental group since the higher homotopy groups vanish.
Therefore, it is reasonable to look for links between the algebraic
structure of the fundamental group and the geometric properties of a
compact nonpositively curved manifold. For a survey without proofs of
results in this section, see also section 6 of [EHS].
416       Geometry of Nonpositively Curved Manifolds

10.1.  Homotopy, homeomorphism, and diffeomorphism type
   In a series of papers T. Farrell and L. Jones investigated the
relationship between the homotopy, homeomorphism, and diffeomor-
phism types of compact nonpositively curved manifolds. The next result
shows that the homotopy and homeomorphism types are identical.

 10.1.1. THEOREM [FJ2]. Let M, and M2 be compact Riemannian mani-
folds with sectional curvature Ks 0 whose fundamental groups are isomor-
phic. Then M, and M2 are homeomorphic.
   At roughly the same time, Farrell and Jones showed in a particularly
striking way that the homeomorphism and diffeomorphism types can be
different.

compact Riemannian manifolds M and M,* such that
  (1) Mn and M,* are homeomorphic but not dif j`eomorphic and

10.2.    Geometry determines fundamental group
   We present some classical results that may be regarded as first steps
in studying the relationship between the geometry and the fundamental
group of a compact nonpositively curved manifold.

10.2.1. THEOREM (E. Cartan). Let M be a complete Riemannian manifold
with sectional curvature K:5 0. Then every element of 7r,(M) has infinite
order.

10.2.2. THEOREM (Preissmann [Pre]). Let M be a compact Riemannian
manifold with sectional curvature K < 0. Then every nonidentity abelian
subgroup of irl(M) is infinite cyclic.

below, although (10.2.2) is also a corollary of (10.3.1). For future
reference we introduce the following.
10.2.3. DEFINITION. A compact Riemannian manifold M with sectional
curvature K:5 0 is said to satisfy property (P) if every nonidentity abelian
subgroup of ai(M) is infinite cyclic.

10.3.   Fundamental group determines geometry
   In the remainder of this chapter we illustrate how the algebraic
structure of the fundamental group often determines the geometry of a
compact nonpositively curved manifold. The first result of this type that
we present is a generalization of Preissmann's theorem (10.2.2) that was
obtained by J. Wolf and Lawson-Yau ([LY]).

manifold with sectional curvature K< 0, and let A be a free abelian
subgroup of it 1(M) of rank k >_ 2. Then the universal cover M admits a
k flat F such that A leaves F invariant and the quotient space F/A is
compact. In particular, M admits a totally geodesic, isometrically immersed
flat k-torus T k = F/A.

   We omit a proof of this result, which is a corollary of (10.3.6).

An algebraic splitting theorem
   It is obvious that if X is a nontrivial Riemannian product, then the
fundamental group of X is a nontrivial direct product of subgroups. On
the other hand, it seems naive to expect that the converse is true, but
this is precisely what happens if X has finite volume and nonpositive
sectional curvature and if ir,(X) has trivial center.

Algebraic rank of the fundamental group
   For any abstract group r one may define an integer rank r >_ 0 that
is determined by algebraic properties of r (see (10.3.13) below). We
then apply this definition to the case that F is the fundamental group of
a complete Riemannian manifold with sectional curvature K:5 0 and
finite volume. This definition of rank r might have no interest outside
the present context. The integer rank ir,(M) is related to the geometric
rank r(M) defined in (1.12) as follows (cf. theorem 3.11 of [BE]):

10.3.11. THEOREM. Let M be a complete Riemannian manifold with sec-
tional curvature K:5 0 and finite volume. Then the geometric rank r(M)
equals rank it 1(M ).
REMARK. In theorem 3.11 of [BE] there was an additional hypothesis
that M have a lower bound for the sectional curvature. This corre-
sponded to the same hypothesis in the higher rank rigidity theorem; see
the remark following (9.3.2). In view of the later result (9.3.1) (or (9.3.2))
this hypothesis can be removed.
   We shall give a detailed outline of the proof of (10.3.11) under the
additional hypothesis that 7r,(M) be finitely generated. This simplifies
the proof of theorem 3.11 of [BE], and this weaker version of (10.3.11) is
sufficient for the next result, which is theorem C of [BE].

10.3.12. THEOREM. Let M be a complete Riemannian manifold with sec-
tional curvature K:5 0 and finite volume. Then the following are equiva-
lent:
   (1) M is irreducible and locally symmetric with rank k >_ 2.
   (2) The fundamental group ir1(M) satisfies the following conditions:
        (a) it 1(M) is finitely generated;

use it to prove (10.3.12). We suppose first that (1) holds. It is then well

Since M has no local Euclidean de Rham factor by (1) it follows from

Riemannian product, then M is a symmetric space by (9.2.5). If M is
irreducible, then M is a symmetric space of noncompact type by (9.3.2)
or (9.3.1).   El

Hence it should not be too surprising that if F is the fundamental group

Visibility axiom and fundamental group
   The title of this subsection describes the next problem that we
consider. The Visibility axiom is defined and discussed in (1.8).
  From theorem C of [E9] we have the following.

10.3.15. PROPOSITION. Let M and M* be compact C" manifolds with
isomorphic fundamental groups and sectional curvature K :!g 0. If the
universal covering of M satisfies the Visibility axiom, then the universal
covering of M * also satisfies the Visibility axiom.
    In the original proof of this result one uses the isomorphic funda-
mental groups to construct a homotopy equivalence f: M - M*. If
f: A? -* i * is a lift of f to the universal coverings, then f is a quasi
isometry that is equivariant with respect to the deck group actions. One
shows that f preserves enough geometry to yield the desired result.
   The result above suggests that the Visibility axiom might be equiva-
lent to a set of algebraic properties of the fundamental group. The first
result of this sort was obtained by M. Anderson and V. Schroeder
in [ASc].

  A second and somewhat simpler idea for recovering the Visibility
axiom from the fundamental group is to try to prove the converse of

10.3.17. THEOREM [BaS]. Let M be a compact real analytic Riemannian
manifold with sectional curvature K s 0, and suppose that every nontrivial
abelian subgroup of 7r (M) is infinite cyclic. Then the universal covering M
of M satisfies the Visibility axiom.
   This result is, in fact, a corollary of something more general. Before

Let M be an arbitrary complete, simply connected manifold with

 10.3.18. THEOREM. Let M be a compact real analytic Riemannian mani-

and let r a I(M) be the deck_group of the covering. If M contains a k flat
